faq.title: Why do smartwatches use green LEDs for heart rate monitoring instead of red light?
faq.description: Oxygenated blood is red because it reflects red light and absorbs green light. Green light (~530nm) has a significantly higher optical absorption coefficient in hemoglobin than red light. Furthermore, green light penetrates the dermis layer precisely where cutaneous capillary beds reside, offering a high Signal-to-Noise Ratio (SNR) that is less vulnerable to motion artifacts during vigorous exercise.

faq.title: How does a smartwatch calculate blood oxygen saturation (SpO2)?
faq.description: SpO2 measurement relies on the differential absorption physics of two distinct wavelengths: Red light (~660nm) and Infrared light (~940nm). Deoxygenated hemoglobin absorbs significantly more red light, while oxygenated hemoglobin absorbs more infrared light. By calculating the 'Ratio of Ratios' (R) of the pulsatile AC signal to constant DC absorption across both wavelengths, the smartwatch mathematically determines the percentage of oxygen-saturated hemoglobin via the Beer-Lambert law.

faq.title: Can smartwatches accurately estimate blood pressure without an inflatable arm cuff?
faq.description: Yes! Advanced wearables estimate blood pressure using Pulse Transit Time (PTT) and Pulse Wave Analysis (PWA). By measuring the time delay between the electrical heart contraction (detected via ECG electrodes) and the physical arrival of the pulse wave at the wrist (detected via the PPG optical sensor), the device calculates arterial stiffness: higher arterial pressure causes the pulse wave to travel significantly faster.

html:
Take off your smartwatch or fitness band, turn it over, and you will see a cluster of glass optical lenses surrounding microscopic light-emitting diodes (LEDs) flashing intensely green, red, and invisible near-infrared. To the average consumer, this looks like simple decorative ambient lighting. In reality, that tiny glass disc is a precision biomedical spectrometer executing continuous optical measurement of human vascular hemodynamics: a technology known as Photoplethysmography (PPG).

Every second of the day, your wearable PPG sensor tracks your resting heart rate, computes heart rate variability (HRV) for autonomic nervous system stress tracking, measures arterial blood oxygen saturation (SpO2), identifies sleep apnea episodes, and calculates pulse wave velocity to estimate arterial stiffness and blood pressure. In this comprehensive technical guide, we evaluate the optoelectronic physics, the Beer-Lambert law of optical absorption, pulsatile signal decomposition, and the machine-learning filter algorithms that power modern wearable medicine.

The Fundamental Physics of PPG: The Beer-Lambert Law

To understand how shining light into human skin reveals biological metrics, one must inspect the foundational law of optical spectrophotometry: The Beer-Lambert Law:

\[I = I_0 \cdot e^{-\epsilon(\lambda) \cdot C \cdot d}\]

Where \(I_0\) is the incident light intensity emitted by the LED, \(I\) is the transmitted/reflected light intensity detected by the photodiode, \(\epsilon(\lambda)\) is the molar extinction coefficient of the absorbing substance at wavelength \(\lambda\), \(C\) is concentration, and \(d\) is optical path length.

How Human Tissue Interacts with Photons:

When light penetrates human skin, it travels through a complex heterogeneous optical medium consisting of epidermis, dermis, subcutaneous adipose fat, muscle tissue, bone, and microscopic capillary beds. Bone, muscle, and skin pigmentation (melanin) have fixed, static optical absorption properties. Arterial blood volume, however, is dynamic!

Decomposing the Photoplethysmogram: AC vs. DC Signals:

The electrical voltage waveform generated by the smartwatch's photodiode detector is composed of two distinct components:

  • The DC Component (Constant Baseline): Caused by optical absorption and scattering from static biological structures: bone, muscle, venous blood, and tissue fluids. This DC baseline changes very slowly over minutes or hours due to ambient temperature shifts and vasomotor tone.
  • The AC Component (Pulsatile Modulated Signal): With every ventricular contraction of the human heart (systole), a pressure pulse wave travels through the vascular tree. Arteries and capillaries in your wrist expand with oxygenated blood, increasing the optical path length (\(d\)) and total hemoglobin concentration. Because more light is absorbed during systole, less light reflects back to the photodiode. During diastole, blood volume relaxes, and light absorption drops. The resulting high-frequency AC ripple—typically accounting for just 0.5% to 2% of total light signal—is the raw pulse waveform!

For more insights into how mobile hardware processes continuous real-time biosignals, explore our technical breakdown of ARMv9 mobile processors and DSP vector execution.

Why Green Light (530nm) Dominates Heart Rate Tracking

A common question among consumers is: "Why does my Apple Watch or Garmin flash bright green during workouts instead of red?" The answer lies in the optical absorption spectrum of human hemoglobin:

  • Extreme Hemoglobin Extinction Coefficient: Blood is red because it reflects red wavelengths while absorbing green light. Oxygenated hemoglobin (\(HbO_2\)) exhibits a massive optical absorption peak in the green spectrum around 525nm to 535nm. The absorption coefficient of hemoglobin in green light is orders of magnitude higher than in red or near-infrared bands.
  • Optimal Dermal Penetration Depth: Red and infrared light have long wavelengths that penetrate deeply into subcutaneous tissue, bone, and deep venous pools, where motion artifacts cause massive signal distortion. Green light penetrates approximately 1.0 to 1.5 millimeters into the skin: reaching the dense, highly pulsatile capillary loops of the papillary and reticular dermis while remaining shallow enough to reject deep muscle movement artifacts during intense running or cycling.

The Mathematics of SpO2 Blood Oxygen Measurement: Ratio-of-Ratios

While green light is optimal for counting heartbeat pulses, it cannot determine blood oxygen saturation because both oxygenated hemoglobin (\(HbO_2\)) and deoxygenated hemoglobin (\(Hb\)) absorb green light similarly. To measure Peripheral Capillary Oxygen Saturation (SpO2), smartwatches deploy a dual-wavelength spectrophotometer utilizing Red Light (660nm) and Near-Infrared Light (940nm).

The Optical Difference:

  • Deoxygenated Hemoglobin (\(Hb\)): Absorbs significantly more Red Light (660nm) than Infrared.
  • Oxygenated Hemoglobin (\(HbO_2\)): Absorbs significantly more Near-Infrared Light (940nm) than Red.

The Ratio-of-Ratios Calculation:

The smartwatch rapidly alternates between firing the Red LED and the Infrared LED hundreds of times per second. For each wavelength, the photodiode measures the pulsatile AC amplitude and normalizes it against the static DC baseline:

\[R = rac{\left( rac{AC_{red}}{DC_{red}} ight)}{\left( rac{AC_{ir}}{DC_{ir}} ight)}\]

The dimensionless value \(R\) (the Ratio of Ratios) is mathematically correlated to physiological arterial oxygen saturation:

  • At \(R pprox 0.4\), blood oxygen saturation is approximately 100%.
  • At \(R pprox 1.0\), saturation drops to approximately 85%.
  • At \(R pprox 2.0\), saturation plummets to zero.

By mapping \(R\) against rigorous clinical calibration curves, your smartwatch calculates your blood oxygen percentage with an accuracy of \(\pm 2\%\), alerting users to dangerous hypoxemia and obstructive sleep apnea.

Cuffless Blood Pressure via Pulse Transit Time (PTT)

The latest frontier in wearable sensor engineering is Cuffless Continuous Blood Pressure Estimation. Traditional blood pressure measurement requires an uncomfortable inflatable pneumatic arm cuff (sphygmomanometer) that occludes the brachial artery.

Advanced smartwatches (like Samsung Galaxy Watch series) estimate arterial pressure by measuring Pulse Transit Time (PTT) and Pulse Wave Velocity (PWV):

  1. The user touches the metal watch bezel, completing an electrical circuit that records a single-lead Electrocardiogram (ECG). The ECG detects the instantaneous electrical depolarization of the heart ventricles: the sharp R-peak.
  2. Concurrently, the optical PPG sensor on the bottom of the watch monitors the radial capillary bed in the wrist, detecting the physical arrival of the resulting pressure pulse wave (the PPG Systolic Peak).
  3. The time delay between the electrical R-peak and the physical optical pulse arrival is the Pulse Transit Time (PTT) (typically 150 to 250 milliseconds).

Under the Moens-Korteweg equation, pulse wave velocity through an elastic arterial vessel is directly proportional to the elastic modulus (stiffness) of the arterial wall. When blood pressure rises, arterial walls stretch and stiffen, causing the pulse wave to travel significantly faster, shortening the PTT! By tracking PTT shifts against a baseline clinical calibration, the smartwatch estimates systolic and diastolic blood pressure trends without an inflatable cuff.

Defeating Motion Artifacts: Accelerometers and Adaptive Kalman Filtering

The single greatest enemy of wearable PPG accuracy is Motion Artifacts. When a runner's arm swings back and forth during a marathon, the mechanical impact causes the watch chassis to shift microscopic distances against the skin. Fluid blood inside tissue sloshes due to inertial forces, creating optical absorption fluctuations that completely overwhelm the tiny 1% cardiac AC ripple.

Modern wearables defeat motion artifacts through multi-sensor fusion:

  • 3-Axis MEMS Accelerometers: Continuously record the exact cadence, acceleration vectors, and frequency harmonics of arm movement.
  • Adaptive FIR & Kalman Filtering: The digital signal processor (DSP) subtracts the rhythmic movement frequencies from the raw optical signal in real time. If the runner takes 180 strides per minute (a 3 Hz frequency), the filter dynamically notches out the 3 Hz motion spike, isolating the true 160 BPM (2.66 Hz) cardiac pulse buried beneath!

Conclusion: The Hospital on Your Wrist

Smartwatch PPG sensors represent an astonishing triumph of optical physics and biomedical miniaturization. By interrogating human blood vessels with multi-wavelength photons and decomposing complex hydrodynamic waveforms, wearable devices have evolved from simple step counters into continuous diagnostic medical sentinels—democratizing preventative healthcare and saving lives worldwide.

Pulse Wave Velocity (PWV) and Cuffless Blood Pressure Estimation

Beyond heart rate and blood oxygenation, next-generation mobile wearable PPG optical arrays are pioneering Cuffless Arterial Blood Pressure Monitoring. The core hemodynamic principle relies on Pulse Wave Velocity (PWV)—the speed at which arterial pressure waves travel through the circulatory tree:

  • When the heart's left ventricle contracts, it expels a bolus of blood into the aorta, generating an arterial pressure wave.
  • The stiffer and more constricted the arterial blood vessels are (high blood pressure / hypertension), the faster this pressure wave travels.
  • By synchronizing an embedded Single-Lead Electrocardiogram (ECG) with the wrist PPG optical sensor, wearable algorithms measure the Pulse Transit Time (PTT)—the exact millisecond time interval between the ECG R-peak (ventricular depolarization) and the arrival of the optical PPG systolic peak at the wrist.

Using the Moens-Korteweg and Hughes equations, the wearable firmware converts measured PTT into arterial compliance and real-time systolic/diastolic blood pressure estimates without inflating an arm cuff.

Adaptive LMS Filtering and Accelerometer Multi-Channel Fusion

The single greatest obstacle to accurate wearable optical biometrics during vigorous exercise (running, cycling, HIIT) is Motion Artifact (MA). When your arm swings or your feet hit the pavement, three severe physical perturbations occur:

  1. The optical sensor shifts relative to the epidermis, modulating the optical coupling air gap.
  2. Underlying venous blood and muscle tissue slosh back and forth, producing optical absorption changes that mimic cardiovascular pulses.
  3. Skin pressure fluctuations alter the local capillary bed volume.

To eliminate these motion distortions, modern smartwatches feed tri-axis accelerometer telemetry into Normalized Least Mean Squares (NLMS) Adaptive Digital Filters. The accelerometer signal serves as a dynamic noise reference channel. The algorithm mathematically correlates the motion frequencies, synthesizes an anti-phase motion noise model, and subtracts it from the raw photodiode current, isolating the pristine micro-nanowatt arterial pulsation even at 180 BPM sprint cadences.
